Yeah, politics just isn't for me.

There are other tragedies in this world, oppression, torture, murder, etc. Palestine is but one place where these things are happening, supported by other people's money and world indifference. Let's all speak out. Let's all call a genocide a genocide. Let's all demand justice for the Palestinian people, the people of Haiti, tge Congo, Sudan, etc.

The press does not exist at the executive branch's pleasure. Access to the White House is not a personal favour but a mechanism through which the public receives an independent accounting of its government.

“The populist emphasis on national identity and threats to it, real and imagined, finds a deep response in voters adrift in a world they no longer understand.” It is hard to imagine a more pompous and condescending formulation. The article—and the accompanying video—seems to perspire a lack of respect for the ideas of the other side. It portrays these voters as an ignorant herd, lost in a modern world they cannot comprehend and retreating into an idealized past to cope, all under the looming specter of World War II.

But this caricature misses the point. These are people with legitimate doubts about the values, priorities, and actions of their government. They have every right to question them, particularly when parties such as the SPD too often present their own positions not as political choices open to debate, but as moral certainties beyond it. So, what's the right answer? There are two distinct problems: (1) how do we keep the world safe from AI and (2) how do we reduce the harmful social and economic effects of AI.

The first problem knows no international boundaries and requires a global solution. The second problem requires a domestic solution in each individual country, because countries differ socially and economically.

Problem 1: We have not had a nuclear bomb used in conflict since Nagasaki. This is due to the formation of the International Atomic Energy Agency and roughly a dozen international agreements like SALT, START, etc. The US and China can lead the way to a formation of such an agency for AI. Sunstein and Toner some close here, but the agencies they propose need to be international.

Problem 2: Each nation will need its own solution. In the US, we need regulation of data centers so that they use only renewable energy that they collect themselves, use closed loop cooling systems, do not emit excessive noise, and are located far from residential areas. We need a good safety net for people who lose their jobs. We need to tax those making money from AI so that Americans can share the benefits of this technology.

OpenAI's Navier-Stokes solution (if it is a solution) took partial work of actual mathematicians, threw 10,000 agents at it, each of them testing a "dumb" hypothesis, until one of them seemingly checked out. It's not hard or brilliant when you do it like that. And it might be helpful if done right. This appears to be an era in which journalism is exempt from impartiality when it comes to AI.

There is no evidence to suggest that OpenAI agents "huggingfaced" anybody. Outside of this ridiculous article, nobody is claiming that AI agents broke into computers to steal data.

What is suggested is that since human researchers used ChatGPT in their work, these interactions could have been used in training of future OpenAI models. This is certainly a possibility. Corporations who pay for AI services get contractual guarantees that their employee usage will not be included in training of future models in order to protect confidentiality of intellectual property. If these researchers were not using an AI service with that guarantee, then it's perfectly possible that subsequent model training included their conversations. Given how AI works, it's extremely difficult to trace output back to specific inputs, so whether such conversations aided OpenAI in later work is likely impossible to say.

Whether this is plagiarism or not really requires some consensus on what that means in the context of AI, but the fix is easy, don't use an AI service without a guarantee of confidentiality.

Of course, this is all about taking credit, not about whether AI helps or not, which it clearly does, both in in the independent work that AI did and also in its assistance of human researchers.

Another article on “drones are the future of warfare” and Ukraine is our guide. Zzzz.

In Ukraine, there are tons of drones, but not much movement of the front lines. That’s Ukraine’s big contribution to the development of war. Drones are the table stakes of stasis.

Too bad wars aren't staged to set up relatively motionless front lines, but to deliver territorial changes that result in political outcomes.

Drones are great at producing footage of tactical kills, but what matters is operational effect. When the Germans rolled through Russia in 1941, pictures of individual tanks on fire didn’t matter. What mattered was that Soviet formations ceased to exist.

Air superiority—unlike drones—doesn't merely give you another way to kill things. It can create the conditions under which your ground forces can maneuver while the enemy cannot. That is fundamentally more useful offensively—and politically—than merely making concentration dangerous for both parties. Alas, neither Russia nor Ukraine has achieved air superiority.

Canada has roughly 24,000 deployable land-force personnel, so putting 2,200–2,500 troops in Latvia isn’t exactly the military juggernaut that headline suggests.

And the readiness picture is hardly reassuring: Canada’s own Defence Department reported just 56% serviceability for key land fleets. Nearly half the fleet wasn’t operationally available.

Then there’s the spending record. Canada finally hit NATO’s OLD 2% GDP benchmark in 2026, after decades below it. And much of the new money is going toward pay raises, infrastructure, and rebuilding existing capabilities; not suddenly creating a larger, more capable force.

For decades, Canada has effectively outsourced much of the hard end of its national defense to the United States while benefiting from the American security umbrella. So a few thousand troops in Latvia suddenly being marketed as “35% of Canada’s entire land force” deserves some perspective.

The core failure is that we have created a consumer economy instead of an investment economy. The focus is on consuming "stuff" whether that stuff is fancy yachts, elegant clothes, or exclusive travel, rather than upgraded infrastructure, advanced training, or scientific research. Investment opens the path to productive innovation, increased capacity, and greater resilience. The cable problem is a resilience failure; a more resilient system would have included some of the monitoring features identified by various comments. In an investment economy communications system outmoded by technology or overwhelmed by a growth in demand would have been upgraded.

 But an investment economy allocates resources differently from a consumer economy, and it would require different structural arrangements challenging the interests of powerful actors. We would be spending more on education, science, and environmental protection rather than remediation. We failed to keep pace with investment requirements in air traffic management, whether that means more sophisticated technology, better management, or more air traffic controllers. Our political system is dominated by people who value consumption rather than investment. Future generations will face ever-greater pressures as our investment proves woefully inferior to our consumption, then we lament system failures with "who could have anticipated this?" We could have, and did not.

Ready for a parable?

Sometime in the 12th millenia, BCE, a fidgety teenager struck flintstone against granite, inadvertently starting a fire. Bystanders were terrified. Next day, the Rift Valley Post reported the incident under alarmist headlines. Opinion writers and media influencers declared the incident a portent of universal doom. Priests and preachers denounced it as Satan's fire, a blasphemous usurpation of God's prerogative to smite with lightning. Politicians demanded an immediate ban on the practice, and severe punishment for miscreates. Tribal councils, Parliaments, and Congresses debated the issue of controlled fire for the next several millennia. 

Over time, mankind suffered and prospered from fire, but endured. Inspired chefs created the delectable dished of the Chinese and French cuisines with their stoves and ovens. Generals settle international issues with bombs and missiles, opting for mutual destruction over negotiation. Demented people shot up schools and churches with automatic rifles. Street thugs put aside their knives and clubs in favor of pistols. White-collar exploiters developed fire protection and insurance rackets. And, so on. 

Artificial intelligence (AI), a computer software simulation of human cognitive processes, is the modern counterpart of the discovery of fire. It can supplement and multiply human intelligence but, like fire, AI is a tool that can be applied beneficially or malevolently.

comments.name: Guillaume

What I loved most about this piece was not so much the promise of Buenos Aires as a destination, but the glimpse of places where people still seem to know how to linger.

A café, a newspaper, a long conversation after a meal, a milonga late at night; these are small rituals, but they give a city texture and continuity. The photograph of the couple dancing especially stayed with me: the quiet concentration in their faces, the intimacy of their posture, the sense that nothing needs to be hurried.

Perhaps that is part of what travel offers, even when we travel only through an article: a reminder that other rhythms of life are possible. In an age that so often seems to reward speed, exposure and constant novelty, there is something deeply appealing about places built around repetition, presence and simply staying awhile.

Thank you for a beautiful piece; and for a brief trip to Buenos Aires.

Reasoning from first principles (I have no military logistics experience):

Parking billions of dollars worth of F-35s and strategic bombers on the tarmac outside or sitting in port in range of enemy missiles and drones is foolish. comments.name: Sam
comments.body: I think that we are overprotecting children today. Parents try to shield their children from everything nowadays and this causes kids to grow up weak because they haven’t experienced any challenges or difficulties. Parents don’t let their children go outside to the local park to play, as a result the kids are stuck inside all day with nothing to do but play on their Ipads and watch cocomelon slop. Like Peter Gray said, “We’re not allowing children to learn that they’re both physically and psychologically tough.” When I see kids today I notice that they are super sensitive and also it is harder for them to get along with their peers. This is a result of parents sheltering children from everything which can lead to them being isolated which leads to them not being able to socialize well. It is important that we let kids go into the outside world and experience the world and socialize with peers.

comments.name: Jentzen Franklin
comments.body: Growing up between the ages of 6 and 9, I was allowed to go out biking with friends as long as I was back before nightfall. In the wee hours of the evening during the summer, when the sun was peeking past the horizon, you’d see a group of kids racing against the clock to make it home. This freedom allowed us to grow and mature, and discover how to handle problems by ourselves without an adult stepping in to solve them for us. Even at the age of 17 I can see the benefits in my life from the freedoms I had as a child.

We would spend all day or afternoon biking around town though every 30 minutes to an hour we would check in with our parents at home. In today's world you have to hold your child's hand every step of the way or you might be suspected of inadequate supervision, like the article said. comments.body: I’ve never had a sleepover, or been able to stay out late, or even be able to make my own financial decisions from when I was a kid to when I was 16. I would like to argue that children need more independence to make decisions and mistakes in this day and age. As a kid, I've missed out on so many opportunities because I was not allowed to go outside. Activities children did many times in their childhood, I have only done once. Just as Peter Gray states that we aren't letting children realize how tough they are mentally and physically, I myself have never realized the capacity I hold as a child. I am stepping into adulthood with a handicap because I never got to experience childhood properly.

comments.name: Connor Holicky
comments.body: Many children today are sheltered by their parents because they weren’t as sheltered, and they’re trying to be what their parents weren’t. In doing so, they’re sheltering their children from lots of important developmental activities, like social interaction,n for example. I had the opportunity to work at Cleveland SAC over the summer, and it was crazy to me how different some of the kids were. On one hand, you had the kids who obviously played a lot and knew they had lots of freedom, and on the other hand, you’d have kids who were scared of everything, partly because they’d never done anything like it before and partly because they thought they’d get in trouble. It’s really sad to see what the overprotectiveness does to these kids, especially when the parents mean well.

comments.name: Rylie Haynie
comments.body: My grandmother was very overprotective of me and my cousins growing up, and it did nothing but make me anxious to do things without explicit permission. When I was young I couldn’t go to the backyard without asking if I was allowed, and most of my energy was spent following rules so my grandmother (who raised me) wouldn’t panic. I think the way she always hovered over me didn’t do any favors to how I grew up. The article discusses “Parents began to control many — or even most — aspects of their children’s lives in order to prepare them for an increasingly competitive society.” but I don’t think this method of parenting actually helps children prepare for life at all. Get good grades, don’t leave the house unsupervised, don’t disappoint parents, all of these only serve to create an anxious environment that makes kids terrified of failure. I wasn’t allowed into a kitchen until I was 13, and only really started to learn how to cook when I was 15, all because my grandmother was terrified of knives. I still feel like I’m making up for lost time today because of how “protected” I was, ideas fueled by fear of experiences and other people generally are actually very limited and should be reexamined.

comments.name: Tommy Saldeen
comments.body: I think we should raise our children based on the area that they live in. Children who live in clean suburban areas can hang out with friends and ride their bikes around with a lot less worries than those who live in poor neighborhoods or cities. Neglecting what children are into or who their friends are has led to countless children dying. For example: gang violence has taken the life of many kids in underprivileged areas. Children are also not very responsible when it comes to crossing the street, which is a problem everywhere but cities can be very dangerous. On the other hand, children need to learn how to be independent and with a parent breathing down their neck all the time, it is hard to learn how to solve problems by themselves. Children learning by themselves will accelerate their ability to help themselves when they face adversity.

I think it teaches them independence and helps them not rely on their parents or other people when they can do things independently. I think people should have more trust in children that they are going to do the right thing when they are alone.

President Lee of S. Korea is right about the need for his nation and the U.S. to end sanctions against N. Korea in order to improve better relations amongst the 3 countries.  However, he is wrong to believe this can be achieved by demanding in return that N. Korea reduce, or put on hold, its nuclear weapons and ballistics programs.  

It's too early to expect such a far reaching change by N. Korea within the next two decades. N. Korea might be more amenable to this if the U.S. withdraws its forces from S. Korea and nearby ocean waters of both Koreas, agrees to a peace treaty, and agrees not to place military forces in S. Korea or along the coasts of  N. Korea and  S. Korea.

In the 2 or 3  decades following the peace treaty, a relationship with N. Korea might be obtained comparable to that now between the U.S. and Vietnam, where the U.S. was defeated.  

To achieve that balance, the U.S., along with S. Korea, might try to promote cultural exchanges with N. Korea such as the one during the last half of the last century when the New York Philharmonic Orchestra visited N. Korea and performed before public audiences there. 

In light of how the U.S. entered and conducted the Korean War, not to mention how it has conducted other wars since and now, it is too early to expect N. Korea to yield any of its current or forthcoming military advantages. A peace treaty now among the 3 parties, accompanied by U.S. military withdrawal, would be a good start, with promise.

comments.name: Invictus

Liability is the first line of defense. But there is a unique problem that A.I. companies face:  There is not enough liability insurance in the world to protect them from the risks their products pose.

Generally, companies have layers of liability insurance to protect them if they are sued due to damage or harm done by their product(s). (Frontier A.I. companies refer to themselves as "labs" and they see A.I. less as a product being built than than a new species being "grown," which could be seen as semantics or a cynical end run around liability).

But most of the rest of the world sees A.I. as a product that they expect to be safe and predictable. Given that, there are more and more calls for liability to attach when frontier A.I. models go "rogue" or exhibit "misaligned" behavior.  But what insurance company or companies would issue a policy to indemnify any of the A.I. companies given the level of possible catastrophic risk?

Knowing the scope of risk, there is only one way for these frontier A.I. companies to shield themselves from liability: nationalization.  

Will that happen? Hard to say. It is a Hobson's choice for them. But with calls for liability growing, it seems like the only path forward to indemnify them from the potentially catastrophic damage their products seem capable of causing.

A year later, we are more sure than before that AI is now an integral part of our company. 

AI's ability to leverage productivity is truly remarkable. We've rethought every process within the company. An interesting side effect is that we no longer have to outsource any part of our work. Developing a complete, complex software system start to finish takes roughly a third of the time that it used to take. To be clear, though, people still play a crucial roles: system design, oversight, quality control, etc.

Things are so fluid right now that It's very hard to predict the trajectory of AI's impact on engineering and business processes. Our strategy at the moment is to stay extremely vigilant about the changes all around and be nimble enough to pivot quickly when needed. And keep debt low!

Look at the lineup of pop culture phenomena we're heading into this fall/winter: a franchise extension of Avatar: The Last Airbender, an "Avengers-style" amalgam season of American Horror Story showcasing characters from 2011, an actual Avengers movie, Grand Theft Auto 6, a Hunger Games movie, a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Harry Potter (now in TV series form), I could go on. 

Culture since at least the mid 2010s has been a constant recycling of millennials' childhoods sold back to us at a premium. We're a generation defined by great promise in our youth and disappointment in adulthood. It's no wonder that our repackaged memories drive cultural consumption. Our memories are the most valuable thing we own (I'm not being figurative or sentimental, check our debt to asset ratios).

comments.name: KSA
comments.body:
At this point, zoomers can indulge in this kind of imagined nostalgia, or they can go vote in November.

I stopped for a drink last night, in my local kind-of-indie bar, and sat next to a group of late-20s restaurant staff, who were relaxing after their shift down the street.  They were on their phones, discussing which internet personalities were less cringe, with the very occasional detour into real life, mostly in order to complain about their absent co-workers.

One guy said his buddy's car had indicted that it was low on coolant.  His conversational partner said, "yeah - well they sell it.  You just go buy more." There was no subsequent attempt to address the question of where the car's coolant, which circulates in a closed-loop system, could possibly be going.

I heard nothing from any of them along the lines of addressing how the built world we live in actually works.

I'm 69, and I know how the built world works, to a great degree, because I've been living in it, so I'm good.

They are not going to be good, I don't think.

comments.body: The major points -- the social media ecosystems and political landscapes of today are fraught and leave younger generations dreaming of simpler times -- are dead on.  Of course, this kind of thing has been happening for generations (Billy Joel mocked it in "we didn't start the fire" in the 1980s).  But it's also hard to find optimism in the 2000s; the "Hope" Obama ran on was a direct response to the really dark times of that period: 9/11, Katrina, Afghanistan, Iraq, Abu Ghraib, the rise of ISIS and horrific beheadings, the 2008 financial crisis, the country's failure to address climate change.   These were not a 'sure there were a few stumbling blocks' but the central narrative.  Vibes were not good (except for tech -- tech was still fun and exciting in the 2000s).  In many ways, this country was more unsettled in the 2000s than it is today, just in different ways.  Hope did last a couple years, until the rise of the tea party set the stage for the MAGA capture of the Republican party, and Facebook et al. figured out how to capture ever more of our attention.

comments.body:
At its core, cringe is when someone likes a thing and someone else thinks they should not. It's on the same continuum as the monetized outrage which has been the Internet's lifeblood for so many years now, but applied to things that by definition do not strongly affect the cringer. 

It's no surprise that people are fatigued by a constant stream of tepid shame-content complaining about other people's taste in music, clothes, ornamentation, etc. Among other things it breeds over time a sense of insecurity, a quiet fear of that inevitable liminality when the cringer becomes the cringee but hasn't realized it yet. It's exhausting and a waste of energy.

If you like finger mustaches that's awesome, get one and have fun with it. I'm somewhat heartened when I read articles like this, about people celebrating the act of earnestly enjoying things, online no less.

The only thing we have to cringe is cringe itself.

comments.body: Graduated high school in 2014. It really was that great. I wasn't a popular kid by any means, but I describe my high school years as something close to "High School Musical". Actually fun pep rallies, $15 concert tickets to see whatever hipster band in small-town Ohio. Social media existed, but it was just something fun and useless to enjoy. We posted photos without worrying about them. Now, I'm slowly taking down years and years of "candid" shots my parents and friends posted without my consent. In retrospect, how could we be so stupid -- even then we were told: "the internet is forever." But back then, we felt like WE were forever. There was hope. Not everyone went to college as they do now. It wasn't some competitive thing. Any college was a fine college. We wore our infinity scarves and Converse shoes. We didn't lock our lockers, and our friends left us notes there between classes. There were cliques and groups, yes, but it wasn't hard to try something new -- just take a new elective next year. You weren't shunned for being bad at something or being a bench warmer. In most cases, everyone was just happy to be there, away from the boredom of home.

What are the chances sea temperatures continue to rise on a more sustained basis and the El Niño-La Nina oscillation becomes more weighted in favor of El Niño, could we see more frequent hurricanes in the eastern Pacific and will their traditional storm tacks change? Southern California would be in little danger even then of storms coming ashore, but could it experience something like what has been happening in Hawaii?

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
Thank you for reporting this. From the article: "“The intensification rate over the past 24 hours  is truly remarkable,” the forecasters wrote in an overnight update."

During a recent summer the tropical storm Otis was near Acapulco in the morning and that evening it made landfall in the city as a catastrophic category 5 hurricane.

It used to be that hurricanes would churn up cooler water at depth which reduced the rate of intensification (hurricanes derive their strength from warm water). Now as the deeper water warms this effect is reduced; so the hotter that we make the ocean the more rapid the ensuing intensification and the higher the maximum storm strength.

Imagine a tropical storm not far from Miami being largely ignored then mere hours later landing as a category 5 hurricane.

With maximum storm strength increasing we need more than ever the best ability we can muster to respond to disasters and to forecast these events that we can manage.

I feel this way because I worked all summer, and I realized you can always work on what you're doing, even if you're doing well at it. Like in the article, Doyne said, “Being a successful self-starter doesn’t mean pulling yourself up by your bootstraps. comments.body: Honestly, I find it hard to ask for help due to the fact that I never really had to as a kid, especially in my elementary years. My elementary schools —since I moved schools a lot— never really.. babied us? We kinda either figured it out ourselves or we were smart enough to know the material right away. There was no emphasis on asking for help and I was typically the kid who knew everything and didn’t need help at the time. It doesn’t really help at the fact that I’m extremely awkward and anxious about asking for help that may seem obvious to others. It’s kinda like an existential feeling of dread on your shoulder when you try to ask for help, well for me at least.

comments.name: Grace Nellessen
comments.body: When you think of asking for help, does your mind wander immediately to the classroom, or to something darker? In the world we live in today, society pushes heavily for independence and focusing on the inner self. What if focusing on the inner self assists in realizing that we actually need help? I remember vividly during my freshman year of high school, I struggled with the transition and was not in the right headspace, which carried over into my sophomore year. Feeling vulnerable is a dangerous thing; it makes you- made me- feel ashamed and more guarded. This emotion could range from experiencing plain helplessness or even to feeling like a burden if you ever admitted it out loud. I will forever be grateful to my older siblings who acknowledged my struggles and urged me to take action. So, when the question is asked of “do you find it difficult to ask for help?”, the answer is simple: yes. Despite this, I wish to empower and acknowledge anyone who is in the same situation as I was. My final encouragement is this: there will always be someone, whether a sibling or friend, who will have your back.

I've noticed some students would rather do poorly in a class rather than ask a teacher for help. I advocate for students to truly take advantage of class time and ask as many questions needed to master a unit. Through my high school years I’ve noticed one of the best ways to do good in a class is to be an active learner, whether that means raising your hand to answer a question or working collectively with your group during projects and board work. I often challenge myself to participate during class even if my answers are wrong due to the idea that you learn best from failure.

As someone who has grown up and lived within the evangelical community my whole life, I have heard about the persecution of the Chinese church.  A state should never control the theology of its people whether they choose to be religious or not (ie atheists nor agnostics should ever be persecuted either). My heart aches for these individuals.

I feel conflicted by this article. It is one thing for an adult Christian to pursue a church leadership position, but children do not sign up for the perils of such a life. She has struggled to the point of spanking and taking out her frustrations on her son.  He is biting himself. Not every religious culture has the same view of marriage, but it does not sound as if she initially wanted to pursue her marriage. Did she really find fulfillment in her role as a pastor’s wife? It is hard for me to be sure. In evangelical circles, it is not unheard of having one’s marriage be considered a sacrifice to the Lord. Her life sounds so forced and without much joy even before her husband’s arrest, yet one cannot deny her courage. The Bible does command joy in the midst of persecution. 

I confess, I do not know if I even believe in a God anymore as I do not understand the biblical portrayal of his justice. Obviously, this is contributing to my feelings. This article states "But none of these systems available are designed to drive cars fully on their own..." but that assertion is false. Tesla is aiming for exactly that and it's nearly there.

Currently, it requires light supervision by a human driver for FSD v14, but not FSD v15, which Tesla is running on vehicles without drivers.

I have my Tesla Model 3 drive me almost everywhere. It's far safer than a human driving (myself or anyone else), it's smoother, and it's quite relaxing. I get to do a lot of sightseeing this way and communicate on my phone, even if I have to look out the windshield about once every 20 seconds.

Given that this article opens with a story about Kyle Shanahan doing something bafflingly stupid (no, this never happened to me) suggests that the Times is not ready to admit that Tesla is saving lives on the road right now.

Waymo is very limited in where it can go, and it still has stupid crashes. Rivian requires lines on the road? Tesla hasn't required lines on the road in years, nor an internet connection, not even a road that matches what is on a downloaded map.

In medical residencies, the final training ground for new doctors, surgeons can be worked to the bone, keeping absurd hours. Anesthesiologists, on the other hand, have strict limits placed on their time. An anesthesiologist explained to me that surgeons DO things during operations where anesthesiologists monitor things. It is much easier to stay awake and alert doing the former. The same is true of airline pilots, who work in a very automated environment. As such, they are strictly limited on the number of hours they can work in the cockpit. In both lines of work, systems management and rapid identification of problems in an otherwise routine and repetitious environment requires exquisite attention that only comes from rigorous training and adequate rest.

Automation behind the wheel will create the same situation for drivers without the extensive training and guardrails that apply to anesthesiologists and airline pilots. On the one hand I am excited for the time when automated driving becomes universal with good failsafe designs. I am also terrified that we are currently not ready for the human/automation hybrid situation the transition to this future will create. As Douglas Adams said, "The trouble with designing something completely foolproof is underestimating the ingenuity of complete fools."

comments.body: Indienne isn’t geared towards everyone. I’m more or less one of them. I can admire the artistry, and I do. I think it’s amazing that some people have the imaginations and the skill to think up and create such rarified forms of food. The labor that goes into it is extraordinary. The results can be, too, though not always, as this review makes clear. In the course of my life, I’ve eaten at a few such places. It was pleasurable. But a part of me finds the whole enterprise wrong-headed. The product, however artful, too is a form of ultra-processing. The ingredients and methods may be totally different from the more ubiquitous, and much cheaper, version, but the impulse is the same. While the product in both cases may be delicious, it’s divorced, finally, from any underlying reality of feeding ourselves (though the high-end version is clearly more nutritious). Maybe there’s a basic absurdity in all forms of ultra-processing. I think there is. We should all be allowed to enjoy what we enjoy and to dine where we want. If Indienne is one’s thing, great. I wish, though, that our food culture would not so often valorize this kind of rarefication and artificiality. Even a four star version like Yamada should give a critic pause. There is nothing to win in AI. AI will eventually become a commodity technology, and the countries that benefit most will be the ones with the manufacturing capacity, energy resources, supply chains, and infrastructure to put it to work. AI will be an enabling technology, not an end in itself.

The idea that there will be one winner in an AI race misunderstands what happens when a technology becomes a commodity. The technology spreads. Its value increasingly depends on what you can build with it. And if AI does significantly disrupt employment, the consequences will not be evenly distributed.

Industrialized countries with younger workforces could face additional pressure if AI begins replacing large amounts of knowledge work. Developing countries that built entire industries around offshoring intelligence and routine cognitive labor could face an even more fundamental disruption if those jobs can increasingly be performed by machines.

But the underlying economic advantages will remain remarkably familiar. Energy. Supply chains. Factories. Infrastructure. Skilled workers. Access to capital.

At the end of the day, the countries that are positioned to manufacture, generate energy, build infrastructure and control resilient supply chains today will be in a strong position to capitalize on AI tomorrow.

There is no AI race where the prize is “winning AI.” The prize is being able to use AI better than everyone else to build things that people actually need.

You have to give credit where it is due: Mayor Mamdani is executing a masterclass in long-term vision to finally get the Sunnyside Yard development off the ground. While President Trump moves with his signature wheeling-and-dealing style, Mayor Mamdani is playing grandmaster chess, focused entirely on the strategic long game for New York City.

The ambition to transform Sunnyside Yard is not new; proposals date back to the 1920s, including bold initiatives championed by leaders like Republican Governor Nelson Rockefeller. But what we are witnessing today carries a far deeper, symbolic weight. It echoes the transformative spirit of the New Deal, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Mayor Fiorello La Guardia united to build historic affordable housing and public infrastructure for everyday New Yorkers. History is repeating itself right before our eyes.

To see this vision rise from the ground would be a dream realized in our lifetime. Beyond the housing, it represents the promise of seamless regional mobility, finally uniting the Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and Amtrak at a single, transformative Sunnyside transit hub. It was a Two Cultures thing where judges and lawyers came from a liberal arts background and were ignorant of things like the mechanical properties of steel.  Politicians have the same problem with computing.  In the broadest sense, it's easy to see that AI development is going too fast because it's a finance bubble.  AI is also getting overhyped in an effort to feed the bubble.  The rest of us are being forced to be beta testers.  There are lots of unforeseen consequences of AI waiting to be revealed.  It's going to be like the Industrial Revolution.  The cultural and economic effects will be huge.  We need to do a better job of managing the change. It is easy to discern the features as feminine.  Additionally, if you look at the painting carefully, you will see that these two figures are almost mirror images of each other.  Each reflects the other.  

Renowned religious scholar Dr. Elaine Pagels views Mary Magdalene not as a repentant sinner or prostitute, but as a key disciple, visionary, and spiritual teacher whose leadership was systematically suppressed by the early orthodox church.  In Gnostic texts, The Gospel of Philip refers to her as a companion of the Savior and states that 'Jesus loved her more than the other disciples.'
